title: Hello, TypeScript!
description: Write a function that returns a personalized greeting string.
objective: Return the string "Hello, TypeScript!" from your code.
hints: Your code must end with a return statement.
String literals in JavaScript use single quotes, double quotes, or backticks.
Example: return "Hello, World!"
starterCode:
// Return the exact greeting string below
return "Hello, TypeScript!";
explanation: The simplest possible program — return a string literal. In TypeScript, string types can hold any sequence of characters. The return value of your code block is what gets evaluated.

title: Sum Two Numbers
description: Add two numbers together and return the result.
objective: Return the sum of 42 and 58. The expected output is 100.
hints: Use the + operator to add two numbers.
You can use variables or add directly: return 42 + 58;
The result should be the number 100, not a string.
explanation: Arithmetic addition with the + operator. When both operands are numbers, JavaScript performs numeric addition. When one is a string, it concatenates — a common source of bugs!

title: FizzBuzz Classic
description: Solve the classic FizzBuzz problem for the number 15.
objective: Return "FizzBuzz" if the number is divisible by both 3 and 5, "Fizz" if only divisible by 3, "Buzz" if only by 5, otherwise return the number itself. Test with n = 15.
hints: Use the modulo operator % to check divisibility. n % 3 === 0 means n is divisible by 3.
Check divisibility by both 3 AND 5 first, before the individual checks.
For n = 15: 15 % 3 === 0 AND 15 % 5 === 0, so the answer is "FizzBuzz".
explanation: FizzBuzz tests your ability to write conditional logic correctly. The key insight is checking the combined condition (divisible by both 3 AND 5) first — otherwise you'd never reach it.

title: Reverse a String
description: Reverse the characters in a given string.
objective: Return the string "hello" reversed. Expected output: "olleh".
hints: Strings in JavaScript are iterable. You can spread them into an array: [...str]
Arrays have a .reverse() method that reverses elements in-place.
Arrays have a .join('') method that concatenates all elements into a string.
explanation: A classic string manipulation pattern: split into characters → reverse the array → join back. The spread operator [...str] also works as an alternative to .split('').

title: Array Sum
description: Sum all numbers in an array using reduce.
objective: Return the sum of all numbers in [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Expected output: 15.
hints: Array.reduce() is perfect for accumulating a value across all elements.
Syntax: arr.reduce((accumulator, current) => accumulator + current, 0)
The second argument to reduce (0) is the initial value of the accumulator.
explanation: Array.prototype.reduce() is a powerful higher-order function. It iterates through the array, passing an accumulator and the current element to your callback. Starting from 0 and adding each element gives us the total sum.

title: Find the Maximum
description: Find the largest number in an array without using Math.max.
objective: Return the largest number in [3, 7, 1, 9, 4, 6]. Expected output: 9.
hints: You can iterate through the array with a for...of loop.
Keep track of the current maximum in a variable, starting with the first element.
Update the max whenever you find a larger number: if (n > max) max = n;
explanation: Linear search for the maximum. We initialize with the first element (not 0 or -Infinity, to handle all-negative arrays) and update whenever we find something larger. Time complexity: O(n).

title: Count Vowels
description: Count how many vowel characters appear in a string.
objective: Return the number of vowels (a, e, i, o, u) in "programming". Expected output: 3.
hints: You can use a regular expression: str.match(/[aeiou]/gi) returns an array of matches.
Alternatively, split into characters and filter for vowels.
Don't forget to handle both uppercase and lowercase vowels.
explanation: Regular expressions are extremely useful for pattern matching. /[aeiou]/gi matches any character in the set [aeiou], case-insensitively (the 'i' flag), globally (the 'g' flag means find ALL matches, not just the first).

title: Flatten a Nested Array
description: Flatten a one-level nested array into a single array.
objective: Return [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]] flattened to [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. Return as JSON string.
hints: Array.prototype.flat() flattens one level by default.
You could also use concat with spread: [].concat(...arr)
Return JSON.stringify(result) so the output can be compared as a string.
explanation: Array.prototype.flat() was added in ES2019. It flattens nested arrays by one level. For deeper nesting, use flat(Infinity). The JSON.stringify lets us compare array output as a string.

title: Capitalize Words
description: Capitalize the first letter of every word in a sentence.
objective: Return "hello world from typescript" with each word capitalized. Expected: "Hello World From Typescript".
hints: Split the sentence into words using .split(' ').
For each word, capitalize the first character: word[0].toUpperCase() + word.slice(1)
Join the words back with .join(' ').
explanation: A map transformation on an array of words. Each word gets its first character uppercased and the rest sliced unchanged. This pattern (split → transform → join) is a common string manipulation technique.

title: Remove Duplicates
description: Remove duplicate values from an array.
objective: Return [1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5] with duplicates removed as JSON. Expected: "[1,2,3,4,5]".
hints: The Set data structure only stores unique values.
You can convert an array to a Set and back: [...new Set(arr)]
Return JSON.stringify(result) for string comparison.
explanation: The Set constructor accepts any iterable and stores only unique values. Spreading it back with [...set] converts it to an array. This is the most concise way to deduplicate in modern JavaScript — O(n) time complexity.

title: Is Palindrome
description: Check if a string reads the same forwards and backwards.
objective: Return true if "racecar" is a palindrome, false otherwise. Expected output: true.
hints: A palindrome equals its own reverse.
You can reverse a string with: str.split('').reverse().join('')
Compare the original to the reversed version with === for strict equality.
explanation: A palindrome is a string identical to its reverse. We reverse using the split-reverse-join pattern and use strict equality (===) to compare. Note: a production solution would also normalize case and strip non-alphanumeric characters.

title: Fibonacci Sequence
description: Generate the first N numbers of the Fibonacci sequence.
objective: Return the first 8 Fibonacci numbers as a JSON array. Expected: "[0,1,1,2,3,5,8,13]".
hints: Start with [0, 1]. Each subsequent number is the sum of the two before it.
Use a loop: for (let i = 2; i < n; i++) { seq.push(seq[i-1] + seq[i-2]); }
Return JSON.stringify(result) for comparison.
explanation: The Fibonacci sequence demonstrates iterative array building. Each element depends on the previous two. We seed the array with [0, 1] and build from index 2 onward. This O(n) iterative approach is far more efficient than naive recursion.

title: Object Key Count
description: Count the number of keys in an object.
objective: Return the number of keys in the given person object. Expected output: 4.
hints: Object.keys(obj) returns an array of all enumerable own property names.
Use .length on the resulting array to count them.
Alternatively: Object.keys(obj).length
explanation: Object.keys() is one of three Object static methods for inspecting properties (alongside Object.values() and Object.entries()). It returns only own enumerable properties, not inherited ones from the prototype chain.

title: Filter and Map Chain
description: Filter an array, then transform the remaining items.
objective: From [1..10], filter even numbers, then square each. Return as JSON. Expected: "[4,16,36,64,100]".
hints: Use .filter(n => n % 2 === 0) to keep only even numbers.
Chain .map(n => n * n) to square each remaining number.
Return JSON.stringify(result) for comparison.
explanation: Method chaining makes functional array transformations readable. filter() creates a new array with elements that pass the test, then map() transforms each remaining element. Neither mutates the original array — a key principle of functional programming.

title: Deep Object Merge
description: Merge two flat objects together, with the second object's values taking priority.
objective: Merge {a: 1, b: 2} and {b: 3, c: 4}. Return JSON. Expected: "{\"a\":1,\"b\":3,\"c\":4}".
hints: The spread operator can merge objects: { ...obj1, ...obj2 }
Later properties override earlier ones when spreading.
Return JSON.stringify(result) for comparison.
explanation: The object spread operator {...obj} creates a shallow copy of an object's properties. When two spreads share a key, the later one wins. This is the modern alternative to Object.assign({}, obj1, obj2) and is widely used for configuration merging and immutable state updates.
